problem: VLN on R2R is defined over a sparse nav-graph of panoramas, which gives agents a known topology, an oracle navigator that teleports between nodes 2.25 m apart on average, and perfect localization. It is therefore a poor proxy for real robots, and it is unclear how much reported VLN progress depends on these hidden assumptions.
motivation: Real instruction-following robots must choose low-level actions, avoid obstacles, and cope with long, poorly framed egocentric observation streams, and they have no map or pose. None of this can be studied on a nav-graph, so integrative studies of language agents with control, mapping and localization are impossible there. The authors observe that a random-heading-and-forward agent reaches 16.3% SR in nav-graph VLN, which suggests a strong structural prior that inflates performance.
key_idea: Lift R2R instructions and trajectories into continuous, reconstructed Matterport3D meshes in Habitat (VLN-CE), where agents act with low-level forward/turn/stop actions from egocentric RGB-D and no pose. Then benchmark standard VLN models and training tricks in this setting.
insight: Without the nav-graph, trivial agents collapse: random and hand-crafted agents get about 3% SR versus 16.3% for a hand-crafted agent in VLN. Depth is essential: Seq2Seq without depth gets 0.04 SR and without any vision 0.00 SR on val-unseen, versus 0.20 for full RGB-D; the No-Instruction and No-Image models still reach 0.17 SR, showing trajectory regularities and weak instruction grounding. Of the VLN training tricks, only DAgger helps on its own (+0.03–0.05 SPL). The progress monitor and speaker augmentation each hurt alone, because the progress monitor overfits without augmented data (val loss 0.67 vs 0.47); combining PM+Aug pretraining with DAgger fine-tuning gives the best model. When paths are mapped back to the nav-graph, the same kind of cross-modal model trails RCM by a wide margin (0.21 vs 0.38 test SPL), even after allowing for about 10 SPL lost in conversion.
method: Trajectory transfer: each R2R panorama node is projected to the nearest navigable floor point by casting a 2 m downward ray and projecting to the mesh at fixed intervals, keeping the point with minimal horizontal displacement (max 0.5 m), plus manual fixes; 98.3% of nodes transfer. Trajectories are kept only if A* shortest paths reach each consecutive waypoint within 0.5 m (77% of R2R), giving 4475 VLN-CE trajectories with an average of 55.88 low-level actions.
Task spec: LoCoBot-like agent with a single forward 256x256 RGB-D camera (90° HFOV), actions FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN-LEFT / TURN-RIGHT 15° / STOP, no GPS/compass, simulated in Habitat on MP3D.

Encoders: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 spatial features for RGB; a ResNet-50 depth encoder pretrained on DD-PPO PointNav; GloVe word embeddings with an LSTM (Seq2Seq) or BiLSTM (CMA) instruction encoder.
Seq2Seq baseline: a GRU policy over [mean-pooled RGB, flattened depth features, final instruction state] that outputs softmax over the 4 actions.

Cross-Modal Attention (CMA): a first GRU tracks the visual history plus the previous action embedding. Its state attends over the BiLSTM instruction states (scaled dot-product), and the attended instruction then attends over RGB and depth spatial features. A second GRU consumes the attended features, the previous action and the first GRU's state to predict the action.

Training: teacher forcing with inflection weighting (coefficient 3.2). DAgger with β=0.75^n, 5k trajectories per round and 4 epochs over the aggregated set. Progress-monitor MSE auxiliary loss. About 150k EnvDrop speaker-generated trajectories converted to continuous. The best model pretrains with IL+PM+Aug, then fine-tunes with DAgger (β=0.75^{n+1}) on the original data.
Nav-graph back-conversion: a continuous path is snapped step-by-step to the nearest node within {current node ∪ neighbors} so it can be evaluated on the R2R leaderboard.

numbers_note: All metrics except TL/NE are printed as 0-1 fractions in the paper and were converted to 0-100 here. No R2R-CE test-split results are reported; the VLN-CE test server did not yet exist. Early stopping and model selection were done on val-unseen. Table 2 additionally reports input-modality ablations of Seq2Seq (No Image / No Depth / No Vision / No Instruction) and random/hand-crafted baselines on R2R-CE val-seen/val-unseen; these are not listed above.
results: The best model, Cross-Modal Attention with progress monitor + EnvDrop augmentation pretraining and DAgger fine-tuning, reaches SR 0.32 / SPL 0.30 on VLN-CE (R2R-CE) val-unseen. This beats the Seq2Seq baseline (0.20 / 0.18), the full-trick Seq2Seq (0.25 / 0.22), and random/hand-crafted agents (~0.03 SR); the agent takes about 88 actions per episode. When its continuous paths are converted to the nav-graph, it scores only 0.21 SPL on the R2R test set, versus 0.38 for the architecturally similar RCM and 0.47 for EnvDrop/Back-Translation. The authors attribute most of the gap to the implicit nav-graph prior, even after accounting for about 10 SPL lost in conversion.
limitations: Only 77% of R2R trajectories (4475) transfer to the reconstructed meshes because of mesh holes and moved objects, so the dataset is smaller than R2R and the nav-graph comparison is biased against the continuous agent.

Purely end-to-end reactive policies with a narrow 90° egocentric view: no mapping, no waypoint/modular control, and no real-robot or actuation-noise evaluation. Absolute performance stays low (~30% SR val-unseen).
Model selection by early stopping on val-unseen; no held-out test evaluation in continuous environments is reported.
